ModelVariations.Description: DeFever designs were produced by different yards and in multiple propulsion/layout configurations; individual hull documentation controls builder, engine package and arrangement.

ModelCharacter: An early wooden Arthur DeFever passagemaker from the pre-fiberglass era, built in Japan with deep-displacement proportions, tri-cabin accommodation and economical single-diesel propulsion. It belongs to DeFever's original offshore-cruising lineage rather than the later Taiwanese fiberglass trawlers.
DesignLineage: Arthur DeFever's earliest private cruising designs were full-displacement 38–54-foot boats created for the Offshore Cruising Society in the 1960s.
Many early examples were built of wood in Japan by yards including Oriental Boat Company.
Surviving boats are documented as DeFever 38 Passagemakers / 38 tri-cabins; DeFever Cruisers separately tracks them as 'DF38 Wood'.
This 38 should not be conflated with the later fiberglass 40/41 trawlers even though owners sometimes describe those hull families as closely related.
OwnershipCharacter: The single-diesel machinery can be exceptionally economical, but wooden-hull ownership is specialist work. Planking, frames, fastenings, decks and insurance availability matter more than engine complexity, and every surviving boat should be treated as an individual historic vessel.

You require conventional 37-foot haul-out/transport options
You want fast cruise speeds or sporty handling

ModelVariations.Name: GH37 versus N37 layout
ModelVariations.Description: GH37 and N37 share principal dimensions and machinery but use materially different interior/deck arrangements; the N37 emphasizes couple cruising while the GH37 maximizes multi-level liveaboard volume.

ModelCharacter: The lower-profile sister to the GH37, sharing the same huge 15'10" beam, shallow full-displacement hull and twin 54 hp diesels but packaged as a more conventional long-range cruiser rather than the GH's raised-pilothouse condo-like liveaboard.
DesignLineage: Mirage launched the first N37 in October 2001 after the success of the GH37 and GH47.
The N37 uses the same broad Great Harbour stability/shallow-draft design philosophy but with a lower, more conventional deckhouse arrangement.
Factory literature offered an optional flybridge while preserving extensive boat-deck space.
The N37 demonstrated offshore capability with a 2002 Bermuda passage while remaining optimized for inland/coastal cruising.
OwnershipCharacter: Twin small diesels, shallow draft and enormous storage make it an unusually capable couple's cruiser. The 15'10" beam and 47,000–48,000-pound loaded displacement remain the dominant marina/haul-out constraints.

Strengths: Heavy fiberglass construction
Purpose-built convertible layout
Strong Hatteras owner and parts support
